edits.definition: Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose programming language, created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991, designed for readability with its clean, indentation-based syntax. It is dynamically typed — a variable's type is decided at run time — supports multiple paradigms (procedural, object-oriented and functional), and ships with a large standard library plus free third-party packages, which is why it serves beginners and production systems alike, from scripting to web backends and data science.
edits.walkthrough_append: Then judge the features as an examiner does, one exam-style pairing at a time: interpreted means each statement is translated and executed at run time, so testing is quick — type a line, see the result; dynamic typing means the same name may hold 10 today and a string tomorrow, so no type declarations are written. Balance the praise with the cost: interpreted execution is slower than compiled C, and readability has a rulebook — indentation is not decoration but syntax. Exam takeaway: match each feature to its practical consequence — interpreted gives quick edit-run cycles, dynamic typing gives flexible variables, libraries give ready tools. Self-check: list five Python features and, for each, one sentence on how it changes the way a program is written or tested.

edits.definition: Decomposition is the problem-solving strategy of splitting a complex problem into smaller, self-contained sub-problems that can be understood, solved and tested independently, and then combined to produce the solution of the original problem. A marks-averaging program decomposes into input, summation, division and output; a school timetable decomposes into class lists, teacher availability and period allocation. Decomposition reduces the mental load of a large task, lets different sub-problems be tackled by different people, and turns each solved piece into a reusable building block.
edits.walkthrough_append: Stress-test the strategy on a bigger case: a railway reservation system decomposes into searching trains, checking seat availability, storing passenger details, computing fares and printing tickets — five sub-problems, each with its own inputs and outputs, each testable alone before the pieces join. Notice the two gains beyond clarity: reuse (the fare computation serves any route) and parallel work (different teams build different modules). Exam takeaway: decompose by asking 'what are the independent jobs inside this task?' and check that each sub-problem has a clear input and output. Self-check: decompose 'prepare the annual school sports day' into four sub-problems, and name one input and one output for each.

edits.definition: A dictionary in Python is a mutable, unordered (insertion-ordered from Python 3.7) collection of key-value pairs, written in curly braces as {key: value, ...}, where each key must be unique and immutable — strings, numbers and tuples qualify, lists do not. Lookup, insertion and deletion run by key rather than by position, which makes the dictionary the natural structure for named records such as a phone book or a marks sheet. Because keys act as labels instead of index numbers, the data is read by meaning, not by location.
edits.walkthrough_append: Grow the empty braces into a working record one line at a time: contacts = {} starts empty, contacts["Amit"] = 9876543210 inserts a pair, contacts["Amit"] = 9110000000 overwrites the value because the key already exists, and del contacts["Amit"] removes the pair. Now feel the constraint: contacts[[1,2]] = "x" fails, because a list cannot serve as a key — keys must be immutable so that their hash never changes. Exam takeaway: dictionaries store key-value pairs, keys are unique and immutable, values are neither; access runs by key, never by position. Self-check: create a dictionary of three friends' birthday months, update one entry, and explain in a line why ["March", 7] cannot be used as a key.

edits.definition: An if-else statement is a two-way selection structure that tests a Boolean condition and executes exactly one of two statement blocks: the if block when the condition evaluates to True, the else block when it evaluates to False. The syntax is the keyword if, the condition, a colon, an indented block; the else, a colon, and a second indented block. Because the condition must be True or False, exactly one branch runs for every input — never both and never neither — which is what makes the structure the workhorse of decision-making in programs.
edits.walkthrough_append: Trace the library-fine example with a pen: for days_late = 0, the condition days_late > 0 evaluates to False, so control jumps past the if block and the else block prints 'No fine'; for days_late = 3 the same condition is True, the fine block runs, and the else block is skipped entirely. Mark on the trace that the condition is tested once, before either block. Exam takeaway: if-else selects exactly one of two paths; the colon and the indentation are syntax, not style, and the condition is always a Boolean expression. Self-check: write an if-else that prints 'Pass' for marks 33 or more and 'Fail' otherwise, then trace it for marks = 32 and marks = 33.

edits.definition: Variable scope is the region of a program in which a name refers to a particular variable. A variable created inside a function has local scope — it exists only while that function runs and is invisible outside it; a variable created outside all functions has global scope — it can be read anywhere in the program, including inside functions. When a name is used inside a function, Python first looks for a local variable of that name; only if none exists does it use the global one, which is how one function's total_score can silently differ from another's.
edits.walkthrough_append: Watch the shadow fall: outside, total_score = 100; inside a function, total_score = 0 is assigned — from that line onward the name inside the function means the local 0, and the global 100 is untouched, because assignment creates a local unless told otherwise. Reading is the opposite: a function with no local total_score happily prints the global 100. Exam takeaway: assignment inside a function makes a variable local; only reading falls back to the global; and the two same-named variables never interfere because they are different objects. Self-check: predict the printed output of a program where a global count = 5 is read in one function and reassigned count = 0 in another, then verify by tracing each function separately.

edits.definition: A list in Python is an ordered, mutable collection of elements written inside square brackets, such as [95, 87, 92, 78]. Each element sits at an integer index counted from 0 at the front, so marks[0] is 95; negative indexing counts from the end, so marks[-1] is the last element and marks[-2] the second last. The built-in function len() returns the number of elements. Because the list is ordered, positions never change unless the list itself is modified, which makes indexing the reliable way to reach any element directly.
edits.walkthrough_append: Predict before running on the marks list: marks[1] is 87 (index 1 is the second element, never the first), marks[-2] is 92 (second from the end), and len(marks) is 4, so the valid indices run 0 to 3 — asking for marks[4] raises an IndexError, the classic boundary error. Note that negative indexing removes the arithmetic: the last element is always name[-1] whatever the length. Exam takeaway: indexing starts at 0, negatives count from the end, and len() fixes the valid range 0 to len − 1. Self-check: for colours = ["red", "green", "blue"], write the values of colours[0], colours[-1] and colours[3], and state what the third expression does.

edits.definition: Flowchart symbols are the standard geometric shapes used to draw an algorithm: the oval (terminal) marks start and end, the parallelogram marks input and output, the rectangle marks a process or computation, the diamond marks a decision with True/False branches, the small circle is a connector joining distant parts of the chart, and flow arrows fix the direction of control. Because each shape carries a fixed meaning, any reader can trace the algorithm without a word of explanation — the shape itself is the statement. A flowchart drawn only from these symbols is language-independent: the same chart becomes Python, C or pseudocode with equal ease.
edits.walkthrough_append: Draw one full chart to bind the shapes: ovals top and bottom for START and STOP; a parallelogram reading two numbers; a rectangle computing their sum; a parallelogram printing it; arrows throughout. Then branch it: a diamond testing 'is marks >= 33?' sends True to a parallelogram printing 'Pass' and False to one printing 'Fail', both arrows rejoining before the final oval. Exam takeaway: oval = terminal, parallelogram = input/output, rectangle = process, diamond = decision, arrows = flow; a diamond always has exactly two labelled exits. Self-check: draw a flowchart that reads a number, decides whether it is even or odd, and prints the verdict — using each of the four main symbols at least once.

edits.definition: The three fundamental Boolean operations work on True and False values: AND (conjunction) returns True only when both inputs are True; OR (disjunction) returns True when at least one input is True; NOT (negation) reverses its single input, turning True to False and False to True. Each operation is completely described by its truth table — a listing of the output for every combination of inputs — two rows for NOT, four for two-input AND and OR. Every complex logical condition in a program, however long, is built from these three operations alone.
edits.walkthrough_append: Evaluate a condition step by step the way the computer does: for age = 17 and has_permission = True, the expression age >= 18 OR has_permission breaks into False OR True, and the OR table returns True; swap to age >= 18 AND has_permission and the same inputs give False AND True, which is False. Count the rows as you write each table — two inputs, four rows; one input, two rows — and no entry can be forgotten. Exam takeaway: AND needs both, OR needs one, NOT flips; the truth table is the definition. Self-check: write the truth tables of A AND B and A OR B from memory, then evaluate (True AND False) OR NOT False.

edits.definition: Pseudocode is a structured description of an algorithm written in ordinary language stiffened with programming-like constructs — keywords such as READ, PRINT, IF-THEN-ELSE, WHILE, FOR, indented blocks and clear assignment statements — without obeying the syntax rules of any real programming language. It captures the logic completely: what is read, what is computed, in what order, and what is printed, while leaving punctuation, declarations and language detail to the coding stage. Its purpose is communication and planning: an algorithm in pseudocode can be reviewed by a reader who has never seen the target language, then translated into Python, C or any other language with the logic already settled.
edits.walkthrough_append: Translate one small algorithm both ways to see the distance pseudocode covers: 'READ marks; IF marks >= 33 THEN PRINT "Pass" ELSE PRINT "Fail"' needs only a colon, indentation and print() to become Python — the logic never changes, only the dress. Keep the conventions straight while writing: one statement per line, indentation to show what belongs inside IF and WHILE blocks, and descriptive names (total_marks, not x). Exam takeaway: pseudocode states the logic precisely but syntax-freely; keywords and indentation carry the structure. Self-check: write pseudocode to read numbers until 0 is entered and print their sum, using READ, WHILE and PRINT, then point to the line you would change to turn it into Python.

edits.definition: File handling errors are the runtime exceptions that file operations raise: FileNotFoundError when the named file does not exist, PermissionError when the operating system denies access, IsADirectoryError when a directory is opened as a file, and OSError (the parent of them all, which IOError now equals) for other input-output failures. Exception handling wraps the risky statements in a try block and catches the failures in except blocks, each naming the exception it handles; the else block runs when no exception occurred, and the finally block runs in every case, so cleanup such as closing a file is never skipped.
edits.walkthrough_append: Trace one robust read in three moods: with a missing name, open() raises FileNotFoundError and the matching except runs, printing a friendly message instead of a crash; with a locked or denied file, PermissionError takes its own branch, so each cause gets its own remedy; with the file present and readable, every except is skipped, the else block processes the data, and finally closes the file regardless of which road was taken. Exam takeaway: try holds the risk, except holds the responses by exception type, else runs on success, finally runs always — cleanup belongs in finally. Self-check: write a try-except block that opens 'marks.txt', prints its content, and handles FileNotFoundError with a message, stating which block runs in each of the two outcomes.

edits.definition: A universal gate is a logic gate from which every Boolean function can be built without any other gate type. NAND (NOT-AND, output False only when both inputs are True) and NOR (NOT-OR, output True only when both inputs are False) are the only two universal gates: joining a NAND's two inputs makes a NOT; a NAND feeding a NAND makes an AND; and by De Morgan's theorems a suitably wired pair of NANDs forms an OR. Since AND, OR and NOT suffice to express any Boolean expression, NAND alone — or NOR alone — can realise any logic circuit whatsoever.
edits.walkthrough_append: Build the set to prove the claim: NAND with both inputs tied gives NOT A; A NAND B through that NOT gives (A NAND B) NAND (A NAND B), which is A AND B; and De Morgan's identity 'A OR B = NOT(NOT A AND NOT B)' turns two NANDs and a third into an OR. Three constructions, and every gate of the syllabus exists from NAND stock alone. Exam takeaway: universal means sufficient for all circuits; NAND and NOR each qualify because each yields NOT, AND and OR. Self-check: draw a NOT, an AND and an OR using only NAND gates, and state De Morgan's two theorems in words.

edits.definition: Tuple immutability is the property that a tuple's elements, order and length are fixed at creation and can never be modified, appended or removed; any operation that seems to change a tuple — such as sorted() or concatenation — actually builds a brand-new tuple object and leaves the original untouched. This is why a tuple can serve where mutable types cannot: as a dictionary key, inside a set, or as a fixed record such as a coordinate or an RGB colour. Immutability trades flexibility for safety: shared tuples cannot be altered by accident, and their hash value never changes.
edits.walkthrough_append: Prove the new-object behaviour with id(): set t = (1, 2, 3), note the id, run t = t + (4,), and the id has changed — the name now points to a fresh object, the old tuple still exists unaltered. Contrast a list: the same append keeps the id, because the object itself changed. Now the payoff: a dictionary accepts (10, 20) as a key but rejects [10, 20], because only the immutable tuple can be hashed reliably. Exam takeaway: tuples never change in place — 'modification' means a new object — and that property is exactly what qualifies tuples as dictionary keys. Self-check: state the output of id() before and after t = t * 2, and explain why a tuple of numbers may be a dictionary key while a list may not.

edits.definition: A Python function returns multiple values by writing them comma-separated in the return statement — return avg, highest — which packs the values into a single tuple object that travels back as the function's one return value. The caller receives the tuple and may unpack it in one line, a, h = avg_high(), assigning each element to its own variable, or index into it like any tuple. There is no separate multiple-return mechanism in the language: packing and unpacking are ordinary tuple behaviour, which is why the count and order on both sides must match, or an error follows.
edits.walkthrough_append: Trace the handover on a marks function: return total, average creates the tuple (450, 90.0) at the moment of return; the call line t, a = compute(marks) unpacks element 0 into t and element 1 into a — a mismatch such as x, y, z = compute(marks) raises a ValueError because three names chase two values. Unpacking need not be complete: result = compute(marks) keeps the whole tuple in result, and result[1] still reaches the average. Exam takeaway: comma in return packs into a tuple; comma in the assignment unpacks it; the shapes must match. Self-check: write a function returning the smaller and larger of two numbers, then call it two ways — unpacked into two variables and stored whole — and print both results.

edits.definition: Type conversion among lists, tuples and dictionaries uses the built-in constructors list(), tuple() and dict() together with the dictionary view methods keys(), values() and items(). Passing a list of two-element pairs to dict() builds a dictionary; list(d) collects the keys, list(d.values()) the values, and list(d.items()) the pairs as tuples; tuple() freezes any sequence into an immutable tuple. Conversion changes more than syntax: a list becomes mutable and positional, a tuple immutable, a dictionary key-accessed — so the target type should be chosen for the access and mutability the data needs, not for looks.
edits.walkthrough_append: Convert one record round the table: marks_list = [("Amit", 92), ("Priya", 88)] becomes marks_dict = dict(marks_list); list(marks_dict.keys()) returns ['Amit', 'Priya'], and tuple(marks_dict.items()) freezes the pairs as (('Amit', 92), ('Priya', 88)). Check each result with type() — the habit that catches the classic error of calling dict() on a plain list of scalars, which fails because a dictionary needs pairs. Exam takeaway: dict() needs pairs, list() and tuple() accept any sequence, and the view methods choose what a dictionary yields — keys, values or pairs. Self-check: convert [1, 2, 3] to a tuple and back, convert [("a", 1), ("b", 2)] to a dictionary, then list its keys, verifying each result with type().

edits.definition: A nested dictionary is a dictionary whose values are themselves dictionaries, storing hierarchical data in levels: students[101]["marks"]["Physics"] reaches into the record of roll number 101, then the marks sub-record, then the Physics entry. Each level is an ordinary key-value mapping, added or removed with the same syntax as any dictionary — students[102] = {} creates an empty inner record; students[101]["marks"] = {} adds a sub-dictionary. Reading requires the full chain of keys, each in its own brackets, peeling one layer per bracket pair.
edits.walkthrough_append: Build a school record two layers deep and walk through it: school = {101: {"name": "Amit", "marks": {"Physics": 92, "Maths": 88}}} — the outer key is the roll number, the inner key 'marks' opens a second dictionary. Read school[101]["marks"]["Maths"] as three doors in sequence; write school[101]["marks"]["Chemistry"] = 90 to add a subject without touching anything else. Exam takeaway: each bracket pair descends one level; inner dictionaries are created exactly like outer ones; and the chain must be built in order, since school["marks"] alone does not exist. Self-check: create a two-level dictionary of two students with name and one subject mark each, add a second subject to one student, then print the other student's name.

edits.definition: Mutability is the property that decides whether an object's contents may change after creation: mutable types — list, dictionary, set and bytearray — can be edited in place while the object keeps its identity; immutable types — int, float, bool, string, tuple, frozenset and bytes — can never be altered, so any apparent change actually creates a new object. The test that exposes the difference is id(): an in-place change leaves the id unchanged, an 'immutability workaround' changes it. Assignment always binds a name to an object; mutability decides whether that object's contents can change under the name.
edits.walkthrough_append: Run the id() experiment on both families: lst = [1, 2]; lst.append(3) leaves id(lst) unchanged — same object, new content — while s = "ab"; s = s + "c" changes the id, because a new string was built and the name rebound. Now the trap this sets: two names assigned to one list share the object, so a change through either name is visible through both; two names on one integer never interfere, since 'changing' it rebinds only one name. Exam takeaway: mutable = editable in place at the same id; immutable = every change is a new object; shared mutable objects are the source of aliasing surprises. Self-check: predict id() stability for a list append, a string concatenation and a tuple concatenation, then state which of the three changes the object's identity.

edits.definition: String concatenation joins two or more strings end-to-end into a new string using the + operator — "Hello" + " " + "World" builds 'Hello World' — and both operands must be strings, since + refuses to mix text with numbers. String repetition builds a new string by repeating its operand an integer number of times with the * operator — "=" * 6 yields '======' — and multiplying by 0 or a negative number yields the empty string. Both operators obey the immutability of strings: neither ever edits an existing string, they only manufacture new ones.
edits.walkthrough_append: Watch the rule bite in practice: "Total: " + 5 fails with a TypeError, so the number must pass through str(5) first — the one conversion every concatenation chain needs. Build a report line the exam likes: name = "Asha"; line = "-" * 10 + name + "-" * 10, and count the new string objects each + created — four concatenations, four new strings, the originals untouched. Exam takeaway: + joins strings only, * repeats, both return new strings, and numbers enter via str(). Self-check: build the line '====Amit====' using exactly one concatenation and one repetition, then explain why "3" + "4" gives "34" and not 7.

edits.definition: The *args and **kwargs parameter forms let a function accept a variable number of arguments. Writing *args in the parameter list collects all extra positional arguments into a tuple inside the function; writing **kwargs collects all extra keyword arguments into a dictionary keyed by the argument names. Fixed parameters come first, then *args, then **kwargs, in that order. The forms give one function definition the reach of many: a single greet(first, *rest) handles any number of additional names, and a single reporter(**options) accepts whatever named settings the caller chooses to pass.
edits.walkthrough_append: Trace the packing on real calls: def total(base, *extras) called as total(10, 20, 30, 40) binds base = 10 and extras = (20, 30, 40), which the body then sums in a loop; def show(**info) called as show(name="Asha", age=16) binds info = {"name": "Asha", "age": 16}, readable key by key. The ordering rule shows its teeth in def f(a, *args, **kwargs): every call must fill a first, extras land in the tuple, named extras in the dictionary. Exam takeaway: *args is a tuple of surplus positional arguments, **kwargs a dictionary of surplus keyword arguments, and the parameter order is fixed, normal, *args, **kwargs. Self-check: write total(*nums) returning the sum of any number of values, call it with three and with five arguments, and state the type of nums inside the function.

edits.definition: The global keyword, written inside a function before a variable name — global total_score — declares that the name refers to the global variable defined outside, rather than creating a new local one. After the declaration, assignments inside the function update the global object, and the change survives after the function ends. Without the declaration, any assignment to the name creates a fresh local variable and the global stays untouched. The keyword is used sparingly: functions that silently rewrite global state are hard to trace, so the standard style passes values in through parameters and out through return, keeping global for genuine program-wide settings.
edits.walkthrough_append: Contrast the paired versions: without the declaration, a function running total = 0 creates a local 0, prints it, and the global keeps its old value — a favourite output-prediction trap; with global total declared first, the same line resets the program's real counter, and a later function reads the new value. Trace both on paper, marking which object each name touches. Exam takeaway: reading a global needs no keyword, writing to one needs global; the declaration goes inside the function, before first use of the name. Self-check: predict the printed value of count after a function without global runs count = 0, and after a second version declares global count first — then state the rule in one line.

edits.definition: Infix to postfix conversion is a stack-based algorithm that rewrites an arithmetic expression from infix form (operator between operands, A + B) to postfix form (operator after operands, A B +), so that a computer can evaluate it in a single left-to-right pass with no brackets. The shunting-yard rules scan the expression token by token: operands go straight to the output; an operator pops higher-or-equal precedence operators off the stack before pushing itself (higher-only, for right-associative ^); a left bracket is pushed; a right bracket pops until the matching left bracket; and at the end the stack drains to the output. Precedence runs ^ above * and / above + and -.
edits.walkthrough_append: Convert A + B * C by hand along the rules: A to output; + pushed; B to output; * arrives, and since * outranks the waiting +, it pushes; C to output; end of input drains the stack, giving A B C * + — the multiplication, though written second, leaves last so it can be applied first. Try the bracket case (A + B) * C and watch the bracket force the + out early, yielding A B + C *. Exam takeaway: operands straight out, operators wait on the stack by precedence, brackets override everything, and the final stack-drain ends the expression. Self-check: convert A * (B + C) - D to postfix with a two-column trace of stack and output.

edits.definition: The with statement opens a file as a context manager — with open("marks.txt", "r") as f: — and guarantees that the file is closed as soon as the indented block ends, whether the block finishes normally or an exception cuts it short. It replaces the fragile manual pattern of open, process, close, in which an unhandled exception between open and close leaves the file handle dangling. The file object is bound to the variable after as, the read, write or append work happens inside the block, and no explicit close() is needed. For text-file work the with statement is therefore the standard, safest form.
edits.walkthrough_append: Run the two endings side by side: in the normal run, the block reads and prints the lines and the file closes the instant the block ends; in the failing run, an error in the very first line — a typo in the filename is caught earlier by open itself, so plant the failure in processing, say an int() on a non-numeric line — still triggers the automatic close before the exception surfaces. The manual close() in the old pattern would be skipped by exactly such a crash. Exam takeaway: with open(...) as f closes the file on every path, success or exception; the body does the work; no close() is written. Self-check: rewrite a three-line open-process-close read using with, and state what happens to the open file if the processing line raises an error.

edits.definition: A string in Python is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters, written as characters inside single quotes, double quotes, or triple quotes for text spanning several lines. Creation is assignment — city = "Delhi" — and the quotes may nest, so "It's raining" needs no escape while 'It\'s raining' uses one; escape sequences such as \n (newline) and \t (tab) stand for characters that cannot be typed directly, and an r before the quotes makes a raw string that treats them literally. Once created, a string can never be altered character by character; every operation on it produces a new string object.
edits.walkthrough_append: Feel the sequence nature before any operations arrive: len("Delhi") counts 5 characters, and each one occupies a position — the groundwork on which indexing and slicing (the next nodes) will stand. Demonstrate immutability early so no later node has to unteach it: city[0] = "M" fails at once, while city = "Mumbai" succeeds because it rebinds the name to a new string, leaving the old object unaltered. Exam takeaway: a string is an immutable Unicode sequence; single, double and triple quotes choose the delimiters, escapes insert invisible characters, and 'change' always means a new object. Self-check: write one string each using single, double and triple quotes, insert a newline and a tab into the third, and state what city[0] = "M" would do and why.

edits.definition: A computer network is a set of two or more autonomous computing devices — nodes such as computers, servers and printers — interconnected by a transmission medium so that they can exchange data and share resources under a common set of rules called protocols. The sharing is the point: files, printers, internet connections and processing power are pooled, and communication runs by electronic message rather than by carrying media by hand. Networks are judged by what they make possible — resource sharing, reliability through duplication, and fast communication — and by what they risk: setup cost, security and dependence on the shared medium.
edits.walkthrough_append: Take one school lab apart into the four needs of a working network: at least two devices (the nodes), a path between them (cable or Wi-Fi, the transmission medium), a network card and switch or router to carry the traffic, and the agreed rules — protocols such as TCP/IP — that let a Windows machine and a phone understand one printer request alike. Then price the bargain: one printer serves thirty rooms (resource sharing), a file copied to two machines survives one crash (reliability), but the same cable now carries every secret and needs guarding (security). Exam takeaway: nodes plus medium plus protocols equal a network, and its benefits are sharing, reliability and speed. Self-check: name the four requirements of a network, one resource a school shares over it, and one risk the sharing introduces.

edits.definition: A queue is a linear data structure organised on the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle: elements join only at the rear and leave only from the front, so the element that has waited longest is served first. The everyday models are exact — a ticket line, a printer's job list, the buffer that holds keystrokes in typing order. Its two ends give the structure its discipline, distinguishing it from the stack, which admits and releases at a single end (Last-In-First-Out). Queues suit every setting where arrival order must decide service order — scheduling, buffering and breadth-first traversal.
edits.walkthrough_append: Contrast the siblings on one scenario: four print jobs A, B, C, D arrive in order — a queue prints them A, B, C, D; a stack would print D, C, B, A, which is exactly right for undo and exactly wrong for fairness. Name the ends while tracing: rear admits, front releases, and no operation ever touches the middle. Exam takeaway: FIFO means first arrival, first service — insert at rear, delete at front — and the queue, not the stack, is the structure for order-preserving service. Self-check: three callers join a helpline in the order P, Q, R and one agent serves them; state the serving order under a queue and under a stack, and say which principle each follows.

edits.definition: A circular queue is a fixed-capacity queue in which the last array position is treated as followed by the first, so that freed cells at the front are reused as the rear wraps around — the wrap is computed by modulo arithmetic, rear = (rear + 1) % capacity. Insertion and deletion still follow FIFO, with front marking the next departure and rear the last arrival; the wrap keeps every cell of the array in play, curing the linear queue's wasteful 'full but empty' state. The one ambiguity left — front == rear signalling both empty and full — is resolved either by keeping a count of elements or by always leaving one slot unused.
edits.walkthrough_append: Walk the wrap on capacity 5: enqueue A, B, C, D, E fills cells 0 to 4; dequeue twice frees 0 and 1; enqueue F now writes into cell 0, not cell 5 — (4 + 1) % 5 — and the freed space is back in service. Then meet the ambiguity: after one more dequeue and enqueue, front and rear coincide; a count variable says three elements wait, so the state is full, not empty. Exam takeaway: modulo arithmetic turns a straight array into a ring, front leaves and rear enters by (index + 1) % capacity, and full versus empty is settled by a count or a sacrificed slot. Self-check: on capacity 4, trace enqueue A–D, two dequeues and two enqueues, giving the cell index of each write and the final count.

edits.definition: A recursive function is a function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller or simpler version of the same problem, and stops when the problem has shrunk to a base case that can be answered directly. Every correct recursion has two parts: the base case (factorial of 0 is 1) and the recursive case (factorial of n is n times factorial of n − 1). Python executes each call by stacking it on the previous one — the call stack — and unwinds the stack as the base case returns, so memory grows with the depth of recursion, and a missing or unreachable base case ends in a RecursionError.
edits.walkthrough_append: Trace factorial(3) down and up: the calls stack as factorial(3) waits on factorial(2), which waits on factorial(1), which waits on factorial(0); the base case returns 1, and the unwind multiplies back up — 1 × 1, then × 2, then × 3 — giving 6. Now break it on purpose: delete the base case and the calls never stop stacking until Python raises RecursionError, the practical proof that base case and progress-towards-it are both compulsory. Exam takeaway: recursion = base case + recursive case + shrinkage; the call stack remembers the pending multiplications. Self-check: write factorial(n) and trace the calls and returns for n = 4, naming the base case and counting how many times the function is invoked.

edits.definition: A while loop repeats an indented body for as long as its Boolean condition evaluates to True, and the test happens before every iteration — including the first. The syntax is the keyword while, the condition, a colon, and an indented body in which something must eventually change the condition, or the loop never ends. If the condition is False at the very start, the body runs zero times, which makes while the natural choice for loops whose repetition count is not known in advance — reading input until a sentinel, or saving until a target amount is reached.
edits.walkthrough_append: Trace the savings loop line by line: balance = 500; while balance < 2000: balance = balance + 500 — the test passes 500, 1000, 1500 and fails at 2000, so the body ran three times and printed nothing extra. Now the zero-pass case: start at balance = 2500 and the condition fails before the first pass, the body never runs — the pre-tested condition is a feature, not a defect. And the danger case: forgetting the update line leaves balance at 500 forever, the infinite loop that every while writer eventually meets. Exam takeaway: while tests first, may run zero times, and needs a change inside the body to terminate. Self-check: write a while loop printing 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, state how many times the condition is tested, and identify the line that guarantees termination.

edits.definition: A tuple in Python is an ordered collection of elements written inside parentheses — point = (3, 4) — that may hold values of mixed types and may repeat values. Order gives every element a position, so point[0] is 3; but the tuple is immutable, so once created its elements can be neither modified, added nor removed. The empty tuple is (), and a single-element tuple needs the telling comma, t = (5,), because (5) is just the number 5 in brackets. Tuples therefore suit fixed records — a coordinate, an RGB colour, a date — where the data means one thing and must not drift.
edits.walkthrough_append: Set the parentheses trap and the immutability rule in one breath: t = (5) prints as 5 — an integer wearing brackets — while t = (5,) announces itself as (5,), a tuple of one; type() settles it in class, so run it. Then try the forbidden edit: point[0] = 9 raises TypeError at once, the immutability speaking; the only 'change' is rebinding, point = (9, 4), which builds a new tuple. Exam takeaway: parentheses create a tuple, one element needs its comma, indexing works as in lists, and edits are impossible in place. Self-check: create an empty tuple, a one-element tuple and a three-element tuple of mixed types, then state what each of these returns: type((5)) and type((5,)).

edits.definition: Append mode is the file-opening mode that writes new data at the end of an existing file without disturbing what is already there: with open("log.txt", "a") the file pointer starts at end-of-file and every write lands after the old content, while in 'w' mode the same open would have erased the file first. If the named file does not exist, append mode creates it, so the call never fails for absence. The variant 'a+' both appends and allows reading. Appending is the natural mode for records that must accumulate — logs, registers, transaction files — because each run adds to the history instead of replacing it.
edits.walkthrough_append: Contrast the modes on one three-run experiment: run once in 'w' and log.txt holds today's line only; run twice more in 'a' and the file holds three lines, oldest first — the 'w' file would still hold one. Check the pointer's position by attempting a read in 'a+' after a seek to the start, and note the ordinary 'a' refuses reads altogether: append mode writes, it does not look back. Exam takeaway: 'a' positions every write at end-of-file, creates a missing file, and never destroys existing content — the opposite of 'w', which truncates on open. Self-check: write a program that appends one line to 'diary.txt' on each run, then state what the file contains after three runs if one run used 'w' instead.

edits.definition: A queue can be implemented efficiently with collections.deque, a double-ended structure whose append() enqueues at the rear and popleft() dequeues from the front, both in constant O(1) time. The usual list runs the same queue in O(n) because pop(0) must shift every remaining element one place left after each departure. Deque keeps both ends fast by storing its elements in blocks linked together, so no mass shifting ever happens; isEmpty is tested with len(d) == 0. For a queue that will serve many elements, deque is the standard container.
edits.walkthrough_append: Feel the cost difference by timing the pattern mentally: on a thousand-element list, each pop(0) shifts nine hundred-plus elements — the queue's every departure gets slower as it grows; the deque's popleft() re-tags the first block and returns, at the same speed on element one and element one million. Write the interface once — from collections import deque; q = deque(); q.append(x); q.popleft() — and the FIFO discipline rides on O(1) at both ends. Exam takeaway: deque gives O(1) append and popleft, list gives O(n) pop(0); the reason is block-linking versus one contiguous shifting array. Self-check: state the time complexity of enqueue and dequeue for a deque-based and a list-based queue, and explain in one line why list.pop(0) is the expensive one.

edits.definition: The three fundamental Boolean operations work on True and False values: AND (conjunction) returns True only when both inputs are True; OR (disjunction) returns True when at least one input is True; NOT (negation) reverses its single input, turning True to False and False to True. Each operation is completely described by its truth table — a listing of the output for every combination of inputs — two rows for NOT, four rows for two-input AND and OR. Every complex logical condition in a program, however long, is built from these three operations alone.
edits.walkthrough_append: Evaluate a condition step by step the way the computer does: for age = 17 and has_permission = True, the expression age >= 18 OR has_permission breaks into False OR True, and the OR table returns True; swap to age >= 18 AND has_permission and the same inputs give False AND True, which is False. Count the rows as each table is written — two inputs, four rows; one input, two rows — and no entry can be forgotten. Exam takeaway: AND needs both, OR needs one, NOT flips; the truth table is the definition. Self-check: write the truth tables of A AND B and A OR B from memory, then evaluate (True AND False) OR NOT False.

edits.definition: Pseudocode is a structured description of an algorithm written in ordinary language stiffened with programming-like constructs — keywords such as READ, PRINT, IF-THEN-ELSE, WHILE and FOR, indented blocks and clear assignment statements — without obeying the syntax rules of any real programming language. It records the logic completely: what is read, what is computed, in what order, and what is printed, leaving punctuation, declarations and language detail to the coding stage. Its purpose is planning and communication: an algorithm in pseudocode can be checked by a reader who has never seen the target language, and translated into Python or any other language with the logic already settled.
edits.walkthrough_append: Translate one small algorithm both ways to see the distance pseudocode covers: 'READ marks; IF marks >= 33 THEN PRINT Pass ELSE PRINT Fail' needs only a colon, indentation and print() to become Python — the logic never changes, only the dress. Keep the conventions straight while writing: one statement per line, indentation showing what belongs inside IF and WHILE blocks, and descriptive names such as total_marks instead of x. Exam takeaway: pseudocode states the logic precisely but syntax-freely; the keywords and indentation carry the structure. Self-check: write pseudocode to read numbers until 0 is entered and print their sum, using READ, WHILE and PRINT, then point to the line that would change first on the way to Python.

Evaluate one layered expression exactly as the calculator should: 2 + 3 * 4 ** 2 % 5 — power first, 4 ** 2 is 16; multiplication next, 3 * 16 is 48; modulo shares the rank, 48 % 5 is 3; addition last, 2 + 3 is 5. Now insert parentheses, 2 + 3 * (4 ** 2 % 5) — the bracket computes 16 % 5 = 1 first, so the total becomes 2 + 3 * 1 = 5 — same digits, different answer, which is precisely the exam's trick. Exam takeaway: the ladder runs ** highest, then * / // %, then + -, all arithmetic binding left to right except **, which binds right to left; parentheses override the ladder. Self-check: evaluate 10 - 4 * 2 and (10 - 4) * 2, then evaluate 2 ** 3 ** 2 and justify its surprising value.
